items.title: M04 - Search, and the pagination it breaks
items.bodyMarkdown:
The support desk has a backlog now. Dispatchers want to type part of a title
or a customer name and see the matching tickets, and scrolling is not an
answer any more.

Adding a `WHERE` clause takes ten minutes. Keeping pagination correct while
that clause is applied is the mission, and it is a harder problem than it
looks, because a cursor is a claim about a position in an ordering. Change
what is being ordered and the claim stops being true.

The fixture in `tests/helpers.ts` was built to punish the obvious
implementations. Six tickets match the word "printer". They are not next to
each other in the full ordering, so filtering after paging returns short
pages. They all share one `createdAt` value, so ordering by the timestamp
alone is not a total order and a cursor carrying only the timestamp cannot
say where it got to. The word appears in three columns and three casings.
And two tickets contain "print" without containing "printer", so a loose
match drags in rows nobody asked for.

Every customer, ticket and dispatcher in this project is fictional.
items.setupMarkdown:
## Get it running

PostgreSQL must be reachable. The starter defaults to `127.0.0.1:5440` with
the `postgres` role and owns two databases, `m04_search` and
`m04_search_test` - separate from the DevPractice platform database and from
every other mission's. Nothing here can reach your learning records.

```bash
cd projects/m04-support-desk-search/starter
cp .env.example .env             # adjust only if your server is elsewhere
npm install
npm run db:deploy                # prisma migrate deploy, onto an empty database
npm run db:seed                  # tsx prisma/seed.ts, safe to run twice
npm run dev                      # http://localhost:3104
```

`.env.example` sets `DATABASE_URL` and a separate `TEST_DATABASE_URL`. Keep
them pointing at different databases: the integration checks truncate and
re-seed the one they use between cases, so sharing a database would delete
your development data part-way through a run.

## The two check commands are different on purpose

```bash
npm run check:baseline   # vitest run tests/baseline.test.ts
npm run check:mission    # vitest run tests/mission.test.ts
```

`check:baseline` must **pass** before you write anything. It proves the
database is reachable, the migration is applied, and every endpoint M02 built
still works, including paging the unfiltered list without duplicates. A
failure there is your environment, and none of it is the assignment.

`check:mission` must **fail** before you start, because `GET /tickets`
ignores `q` entirely and returns everything. Those failures are the
assignment.

`npm run check:all` runs both. `npm run build` type-checks with
`tsc --noEmit`.

## Response shape

Unchanged from M02: `{ "data": [...], "meta": { "nextCursor": ..., "hasMore": ... } }`
on success, `{ "error": { "code": ..., "message": ... } }` on a rejection. The
checks read those fields, so keep the shape.
baselineChecks: npm run db:deploy - the initial Prisma migration applies to an empty database
npm run db:seed - loads two fictional dispatchers, five tickets and three comments, and is safe to run twice
npm run check:baseline - database reachable, tables migrated, health route answering, and every M02 endpoint still correct including unfiltered paging; this must pass before you start
acceptanceCriteria: GET /tickets?q=printer returns exactly the matching tickets and nothing else.
The match covers title, body and customerName, not the title alone.
The match is case-insensitive.
A substring the caller did not ask for does not match: searching "printer" must not return a ticket that only says "printing".
q composes with the existing status filter.
An empty q behaves like no search at all rather than matching nothing.
A search with no matches returns an empty page with hasMore false and a null cursor, not an error.
Paging through a search returns every match exactly once, with no duplicates, at every page size including 1.
The search stays applied on the second page and every page after it.
A cursor reused with different search text does not silently return a wrong page: either it is rejected, or it carries enough to stay correct.
Migrations apply cleanly to an empty database and the seed is repeatable.

checklist.label: check:baseline passes and check:mission fails before I change anything
The search looks at title, body and customerName
Casing does not change the result set
The ordering I page by is a total order, so no row can tie with another
The filter is applied on every page, not only the first
I decided what a cursor from a different search should do, and can defend it
Empty search text and a search with no matches both behave sensibly

hints: Prisma's `contains` takes a `mode` option, which settles the casing question. Then ask what the page is actually ordered by, because that is where the real problem is.
A cursor has to identify one row unambiguously. In this fixture `createdAt` does not, because six rows share a value. Which pair of columns does, and does your ORDER BY use the same pair?

Ask what the cursor is a position WITHIN. If the honest answer is "this specific query", then a cursor handed back with different search text is meaningless, and you have two defensible options: refuse it, or put the filter inside the cursor so it cannot be misused.
items.solutionMarkdown:
Two changes, and the second is the one worth remembering.

**The filter.** `q` becomes an `OR` across `title`, `body` and `customerName`
with `mode: 'insensitive'`, combined with the existing status filter rather
than replacing it. `contains` rather than a word match is what keeps
"printing" out of a search for "printer" while still finding "printer queue":
the substring asked for is present in one and absent from the other.

**The ordering and the cursor.** The filter has to be part of the same query
that pages, never applied to a page after it has been fetched - otherwise the
page boundary is decided before the filter runs and pages come back short.
And because six rows share a `createdAt`, the cursor carries `(createdAt, id)`
and the `ORDER BY` uses the same pair. A compound cursor and a compound sort
have to agree; a cursor on one column with a sort on two is a silent source
of repeated and skipped rows, and it only shows up when two rows tie, which
in a small test database may be never.

**The reused cursor.** The reference solution puts a fingerprint of the active
filter into the cursor and rejects a cursor whose fingerprint does not match,
with a 400. Carrying the filter inside the cursor and ignoring the query
parameter would also be correct and is what several real APIs do. What is not
acceptable is accepting a foreign cursor and answering with a page that
belongs to neither query.

What this solution does NOT claim: `contains` cannot use a plain B-tree index,
so on a large table this search scans. The honest next step is a trigram index
or a full-text column, and the honest way to decide is to look at the query
plan on representative data rather than guessing. Chapter 13 is where that
plan is read.
reflectionRubric: I can explain why ordering by createdAt alone is not enough, using the fixture as evidence rather than as a rule I was told.
I can say what my cursor encodes and why each part of it is there.
I can describe what I decided about a cursor reused with different search text, and name the alternative I rejected.
I can say what would have to change before this search was acceptable on a large table, and how I would know it was needed.

items.title: M05 - A dashboard that asks too many questions
items.bodyMarkdown:
This code works. Every baseline check passes and every response is correct.
That is what makes this mission different from the others: you are not fixing
a wrong answer, you are fixing how a right answer is obtained.

The desk added a dashboard listing tickets with their comment counts and
latest comment. It was fine against five seeded tickets. With a realistic
backlog the page takes seconds and the database sits at high CPU, and nobody
can point at a line and say "that one is slow", because no single line is.

The shape of the problem is the point. One query fetches the page of tickets,
and then, for each ticket, two more go out: one to count its comments and one
to find the newest. Twenty tickets is forty-one round trips. The code reads
perfectly well. The cost is invisible in the source and obvious in a log of
what was actually sent.

So the mission gives you the log. `src/db.ts` emits query events and
`countQueries` records them, which means your work can be measured rather
than argued about. Your job is to make the round trips stop growing with the
page size while the response body stays byte-for-byte what it is today.

Every ticket, comment and customer here is fictional.
items.setupMarkdown:
## Get it running

PostgreSQL on `127.0.0.1:5440`, and two databases that belong to this mission
alone: `m05_nplus1` and `m05_nplus1_test`. Neither is the platform database.

```bash
cd projects/m05-support-desk-nplus1/starter
cp .env.example .env
npm install
npm run db:deploy                # migrations onto an empty database
npm run db:seed                  # repeatable
npm run dev                      # http://localhost:3105
```

## Measure before you change anything

```bash
npm run check:baseline   # must pass now: the dashboard is CORRECT
npm run check:mission    # must fail now: the dashboard is EXPENSIVE
```

Read the failure output before you write code. It prints the SQL that was
actually issued, and counting those statements yourself is the skill this
mission is really teaching. A fix you cannot measure is a guess.

## Do not change the measurement

`src/db.ts` holds the query recorder. It is instrumentation, not assignment,
and the one listener it registers is deliberate: Prisma has no way to remove
an event listener, so registering one per measurement would leak them and
cross-contaminate the counts. Leave it alone.

## Do not change the answer either

The response body is pinned. The mission checks compare your output against
the same dashboard computed independently from the database, including the
cases that catch a plausible wrong answer: a ticket with no comments must
report zero rather than disappear, and the latest comment must be the latest
one rather than whichever row came back first.
baselineChecks: npm run db:deploy - migrations apply to an empty database
npm run db:seed - repeatable seed, safe to run twice

npm run check:baseline - the dashboard endpoint returns correct counts and latest comments, and the plain listing still pages correctly; this must pass before you start, because the starter is not wrong, only slow
acceptanceCriteria: The number of queries issued by GET /tickets?withComments=true does not grow with the page size: a page of 20 costs the same number of round trips as a page of 4.
A full page of 20 tickets costs at most 3 queries.
The response body is unchanged: same rows, same order, same commentCount, same latestCommentBody.
A ticket with no comments reports a count of zero and a null latest comment, and is not dropped from the page.
The latest comment is the newest one by createdAt, with id as the tiebreaker, not an arbitrary row.
The plain listing without withComments stays cheap and does not gain comment fields it was not asked for.
The query recorder in src/db.ts is unchanged.

checklist.label: I counted the queries the starter issues before changing anything
The count no longer depends on the page size
The response body is identical to before, including the empty and tied cases
A ticket with no comments is still in the page
The latest comment is chosen by a total ordering, not by luck
I did not change the measurement to make the number look better

hints: Do not optimise yet. Run the mission checks and read the SQL they print. Count the statements for a page of 4 and a page of 20, and write both numbers down - the rest of the mission is making the second number stop depending on the first.

Two round trips can answer the whole page: fetch the tickets, then fetch the comment data for all of their ids at once. `groupBy` with a `_count` gives you the counts in one query; the latest comment per ticket is the harder half.

For "the latest per group", either sort the relevant comments once in SQL and pick the first per ticket in memory, or express it as a window function with `$queryRaw`. Both are fine. What is not fine is a query inside a loop, however tidy the loop looks.
items.solutionMarkdown:
The reference solution answers the whole page in two queries plus the page
fetch itself.

**Counts.** One `groupBy` over comments, filtered to the ticket ids on this
page, returning a count per ticket. A ticket with no comments has no row in
that result at all, which is exactly the case a naive join loses - so the
lookup defaults to zero rather than assuming every ticket is present.

**Latest comments.** One query fetching the comments for those ids ordered by
`(ticketId, createdAt desc, id desc)`, then a single pass keeping the first
comment seen per ticket. The `id` tiebreaker matters: two comments written in
the same millisecond would otherwise make the answer depend on which row the
database happened to return first, and a test that passes for that reason
passes for no reason.

**Why not one clever query.** A `LEFT JOIN LATERAL` would do it in one round
trip, and on this data that is a smaller win than it sounds: three bounded
queries do not scale with the page, which was the actual problem. Reaching
for raw SQL also costs you Prisma typing at the boundary. The point of the
mission is the shape of the cost, not the smallest possible number.

**What was never true.** The starter was not wrong and the fix did not make
it correct - it was correct throughout. What changed is that the cost of an
answer no longer depends on how much of it you asked for. That distinction is
worth keeping, because it is the difference between a bug report and a
capacity problem, and they are fixed by different people at different times.
reflectionRubric: I can state the query count before and after, for two different page sizes, from measurement rather than estimate.
I can explain why the starter was correct and still unacceptable.
I can explain why a ticket with no comments is the case that catches a wrong fix.
I can say why the id tiebreaker is in the ordering, and what would be untestable without it.
I can name the next thing I would measure if the page were still slow after this change.

items.title: M06 - Inventory, and the invariants that hold it together
items.bodyMarkdown:
A new service, built from an empty routes file. The database, the schema, the
migrations, the seed and the server already work; every endpoint is missing.

Five endpoints: create a product, list products with their on-hand quantity,
record a stock movement, place an order with lines, and fetch an order with
its total.

The CRUD is not the interesting part. The invariants are - the statements
that must be true no matter what a caller sends or how two callers interleave.
A SKU is unique. A movement is a non-zero whole number. On-hand stock is never
negative. An order has at least one line, every line has a quantity of at
least one, and every line points at a product that exists. And placing an
order writes its lines and its stock movements together, or writes none of
them.

Read the schema before you write a route. On-hand stock is the SUM OF
MOVEMENTS, not a column you decrement. That choice makes "never negative"
harder to state, because there is no single value to hang a CHECK constraint
on - and it is what gives every change a reason and an audit trail, and what
stops two concurrent writers losing an update by overwriting a total. Part of
this mission is deciding which of the six invariants belongs in the schema,
which belongs in a transaction, and which belongs in the route.

Every product, price and customer in this project is fictional.
items.setupMarkdown:
## Get it running

PostgreSQL on `127.0.0.1:5440`. This mission owns `m06_inventory` and
`m06_inventory_test`, and can reach neither the platform database nor another
mission's.

```bash
cd projects/m06-inventory-core/starter
cp .env.example .env
npm install
npm run db:deploy                # migrations onto an empty database
npm run db:seed                  # repeatable
npm run dev                      # http://localhost:3106
```

## The two check commands

```bash
npm run check:baseline   # must pass now: database, migrations, health route
npm run check:mission    # must fail now: every endpoint answers 501
```

The starter answers `501 NOT_IMPLEMENTED` on purpose, so a fresh checkout
fails loudly and unambiguously rather than half-working.

## Status codes the checks expect

| Situation | Response |
| --- | --- |
| created | 201 with `{ "data": ... }` |
| invalid body | 400 with `{ "error": { "code": "BAD_REQUEST", "fieldErrors": ... } }` |
| duplicate SKU | 409 |
| line references a product that does not exist | 404 |
| not enough stock | 409, naming the product and the quantities |
| unknown order id | 404 |

Money is in minor units throughout - whole pence, never a float. An order
total is derived from the prices captured on its lines, so repricing a
product later must not change a placed order.
baselineChecks: npm run db:deploy - the initial migration applies to an empty database, creating products, stock movements, orders and order lines
npm run db:seed - repeatable seed of fictional users and products
npm run check:baseline - database reachable, tables migrated, unique SKU index and order-line foreign keys enforced by PostgreSQL, health route answering; this must pass before you start
acceptanceCriteria: POST /products creates a product and returns 201; a duplicate SKU is rejected with 409, decided by the database rather than by a check-then-insert.
A rejected product writes no rows.
GET /products lists every product with its on-hand quantity summed from the movement ledger, including zero for a product that has never moved.
POST /products/:id/movements rejects a zero or fractional delta with 400, and an unknown product with 404.
A movement that would drive on-hand stock negative is rejected with 409 and writes nothing.
POST /orders rejects an order with no lines, or a line with quantity below one, with 400.
An order line referencing a product that does not exist returns 404 and writes no order.
Placing an order writes the order, its lines and one stock movement per line, or writes none of them: a shortfall on the second line must leave no trace of the first.
Line prices are captured when the order is placed, so repricing a product afterwards does not change the order total.
GET /orders/:id returns the order with its lines and a total derived from the captured prices, and 404 for an unknown id.
Migrations apply cleanly to an empty database and the seed is repeatable.

checklist.label: check:baseline passes and check:mission fails before I change anything
For each of the six invariants I can say which of schema, transaction or route enforces it, and why there
The duplicate SKU is decided by the unique index, not by a read before the insert
On-hand stock is summed from movements; I did not add a quantity column
A failure on a later line leaves no rows from an earlier one
An order total survives a reprice of its products
A shortfall says which product and what the numbers were, and is not a 500

hints: Start with the schema, not the routes. Read every constraint in `prisma/schema.prisma` and write down what each one makes impossible. Several of the acceptance criteria are already enforced there, and your route only has to turn the resulting error into a decent response.

For the duplicate SKU, let the insert fail and catch it. Prisma raises `P2002` for a unique violation. A read that checks first and then inserts has a gap between the two statements, and two concurrent requests both pass the check - the unique index has no gap.

Placing an order needs one `$transaction`, and the stock check has to happen INSIDE it and be re-read there. Checking on-hand stock before opening the transaction tells you what was true a moment ago, which is not what you need to know. Throwing from inside the callback is what rolls everything back.
items.solutionMarkdown:
The theme of this solution is that an invariant is only as strong as the place
it is enforced, and the three places are not interchangeable.

**The schema holds what must never be true of stored data.** A unique SKU, a
line that must point at a real product, one line per product per order. These
survive a bug in the route file, which is the entire reason they belong there
rather than in an `if`.

**The transaction holds what must be true across several rows.** An order,
its lines and its movements are one fact. Nothing outside a transaction can
express that, and the all-or-nothing criterion is unreachable without it: the
reference solution throws from inside the callback, which rolls back the order
row and any earlier line along with it.

**The route holds what makes a good error.** A 409 naming the product and the
quantities, rather than a constraint violation leaking out as a 500. The
database decided; the route translated.

**Stock deserves its own note.** On-hand is the sum of movements. "Never
negative" therefore cannot be a CHECK constraint, so it is re-read and
re-checked inside the transaction, where a concurrent order cannot slip
between the read and the write. What this buys is an audit trail and
append-only writes; what it costs is exactly this care.

**Where this is still weak, said plainly.** Two concurrent orders for the same
scarce product are serialised by PostgreSQL at READ COMMITTED only because
each re-reads the sum inside its transaction - under a stricter requirement
you would want an explicit lock or a constraint on a materialised total. M11
is where that argument gets settled properly, with concurrency tokens and a
conflicting pair of writers.
reflectionRubric: For each of the six invariants I can name where I enforced it and defend that choice against one alternative.
I can explain why a read-then-insert uniqueness check is not equivalent to a unique index.
I can explain what the stock ledger buys and what it costs, rather than treating it as the obviously right design.
I can describe what a half-placed order would look like in the database, and what prevents it.
I can say which of my error responses an operator could act on without reading my code.

items.title: M07 - The order that was placed twice
items.bodyMarkdown:
The inventory service works. Orders are placed, stock moves, and everything
commits atomically. It also has a defect that only appears in production,
which is the worst place to find one.

The ordering app retries. Phones drop connections, the load balancer gives up
at thirty seconds while the request is still committing, and people press
"Place order" again when nothing seems to have happened. The API documents an
`Idempotency-Key` header for exactly this, and the client sends it faithfully.

The header is accepted and ignored. A retried submission places a second
order and moves stock again. Warehouse staff are picking duplicates and the
on-hand figures have drifted.

The repair is four rules, and the interesting one is the second. Same key and
same body twice gives one order, with the retry replaying the first response.
Same key and same body CONCURRENTLY still gives one order - and that rules out
the tempting shape, because two requests that are genuinely in flight at the
same instant both pass a "have I seen this key?" check before either writes.
Same key with a DIFFERENT body is a conflict, not a replay, because the client
has reused a key for a different intent and quietly discarding the second
order would be worse than refusing it. And keys are scoped per user, because
two people may both choose "order-1".

Look at what is already in the schema before you design anything.

Every order, product and name here is fictional.
items.setupMarkdown:
## Get it running

PostgreSQL on `127.0.0.1:5440`, with `m07_inventory` and
`m07_inventory_test` belonging to this mission alone.

```bash
cd projects/m07-inventory-idempotency/starter
cp .env.example .env
npm install
npm run db:deploy                # migrations onto an empty database
npm run db:seed                  # repeatable
npm run dev                      # http://localhost:3107
```

## Reproduce the defect before you fix it

```bash
# Place the same order twice with the same key. Today you get two orders.
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3107/orders \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -H 'idempotency-key: demo-1' \
  -d '{"customerName":"Brightleaf Bakery","lines":[{"productId":"prod-ink-black","quantity":2}]}'
```

Run it twice and compare the two order ids. Then check on-hand stock.

## The two check commands

```bash
npm run check:baseline   # must pass now: orders, stock and atomicity all work
npm run check:mission    # must fail now: the retry rules
```

A failing `check:mission` here is the defect, not a broken environment.

## What the mission checks actually do

One of them fires two submissions at the same instant with `Promise.all` and
then counts the orders in the database. A fix that works when the retry
arrives a second later and fails when it arrives in the same millisecond will
be caught, which is the point: the bug you are fixing IS a timing bug, so a
fix that depends on timing has not fixed it.

A replay returns **200**, not 201, because that request created nothing.
baselineChecks: npm run db:deploy - migrations apply to an empty database, including the IdempotencyRecord table and its unique index on (ownerId, operation, key)
npm run db:seed - repeatable seed of fictional users and products

npm run check:baseline - orders place correctly, stock moves, a shortfall rolls the whole order back, and a rejected body writes nothing; this must pass before you start, because the service is not broken, only unsafe to retry
acceptanceCriteria: Two sequential submissions with the same key and the same body create one order; the second returns 200 with the first response, including the original order id.
Two CONCURRENT submissions with the same key and the same body still create one order, and one stock movement per line rather than two.
The same key with a different body is rejected with 409 rather than replaying the first response.
Keys are scoped per training user: two users may use the same key without colliding.
A submission with no Idempotency-Key behaves exactly as it does today.
A submission rejected for an invalid body does not consume the key: correcting the body and retrying with the same key succeeds.
A submission that fails for a shortfall does not record a success: the key stays usable once stock allows the order.
Stock moves exactly once per placed order, verified from the movement ledger rather than from the API response.
Nothing about the non-idempotent endpoints changes.

checklist.label: I reproduced the duplicate order by hand before changing code
Which request wins is decided by a database constraint, not by which one arrived first
The record of the work commits in the same transaction as the work
A replay returns 200 and the original body, not a second creation
The same key with a different body conflicts instead of replaying
A failed submission leaves the key usable
Keys are scoped so two users cannot collide

hints: Read the `IdempotencyRecord` model and its unique constraint on (ownerId, operation, key) before you write anything. Ask which of the four rules that constraint can decide on its own, and which one you have to decide.

A check-then-write cannot work here and no amount of reordering the statements fixes it, because the gap is between two round trips. Invert it: attempt the insert and treat a unique violation as the answer rather than as an error. Prisma raises `P2002`.

Decide where the receipt is written. Inside the same transaction as the order, a failure rolls the receipt back with the work and a crash between the two becomes impossible. Outside it, you have invented a new way to lose or duplicate an order. Then store a fingerprint of the body so you can tell a genuine retry from a reused key.
items.solutionMarkdown:
One rule decides the whole shape: let the database arbitrate, not the clock.

**The receipt is inserted inside the transaction that places the order**, and
`(ownerId, operation, key)` is unique. Two concurrent submissions race to
insert it; exactly one wins, and the loser gets a unique violation it can
recognise, after its own transaction has already rolled back - so no
duplicate order ever existed. It then reads the winner's stored response and
replays it. Correctness does not depend on which request was faster, which is
the only way to fix a timing bug.

Writing the receipt inside the transaction gives two more rules for free. The
work and the record of it commit together, so a crash between them is not a
state the system can be in. And a FAILED submission rolls its receipt back
with everything else, which is what lets a corrected retry through instead of
replaying a failure forever.

**The request fingerprint covers the mismatch case.** A hash over the
canonicalised body, so field order does not matter: a client that serialised
the same intent differently has not changed its mind. A different hash under
the same key is a 409. Replaying the first response there would silently throw
away a real order, and the client would have no way to know.

**The fast path is an optimisation, not the guarantee.** The solution does
look the key up first, because most retries are not concurrent and a cheap
read saves a rolled-back transaction. Delete that block and everything still
works. Delete the unique constraint and nothing does. It is worth being able
to say which part of your code is load-bearing.

**The boundary of the claim.** This makes the EFFECT of a submission happen
once per key: one order, one movement per line. It does not make the HTTP
request happen once - it cannot, and nothing in an API can. Saying
"exactly-once" without naming which of the two you mean is how teams end up
believing a guarantee nobody implemented.
reflectionRubric: I can explain why a read-then-write idempotency check fails under concurrency, without using the word "fast".
I can say which database object makes the guarantee, and what would break if it were removed.
I can defend returning 409 for a reused key with a different body, against the alternative of replaying.
I can explain why a failed submission must not leave a usable receipt behind.
I can state what is exactly-once here and what is merely at-least-once, and say which one the client sees.

items.title: M08 - A report job you can rerun
items.bodyMarkdown:
A nightly stock-valuation report. For every product it writes one row holding
the quantity on hand and its value, then marks the job succeeded. On a first
run, on a quiet machine, it works, and the baseline checks prove exactly that
much.

It cannot be rerun. And a background job that cannot be rerun is a job you
cannot operate, because every retry, every deployment part-way through a run,
and every duplicated scheduler tick is a second run.

Four things are wrong. A rerun after a partial failure repeats work that was
already committed - the unique index stops the duplicate row being stored, so
instead of quietly duplicating, the rerun dies on the first product it already
did and the job can never finish. A loud failure is still a failure. A job
that already succeeded runs all over again. `maxAttempts` and `runAfter` sit
in the schema unused, so nothing stops a hopeless job retrying forever and
nothing delays the next try. And the claim is a read followed by a write, so
two workers can both decide the job is theirs.

The mission checks inject a failure part-way through the run and then rerun,
which is the only honest way to test this: a job that has never been
interrupted has never been tested.

There is also a vocabulary question the reflection will ask you, and it is
worth carrying while you work. This runner is invoked at least once and may be
invoked again at any moment. You cannot make the invocation happen exactly
once. You can make its committed effect exactly once. Say which you mean.

Every product, valuation and report row here is fictional.
items.setupMarkdown:
## Get it running

PostgreSQL on `127.0.0.1:5440`, with `m08_inventory` and
`m08_inventory_test` belonging to this mission alone.

```bash
cd projects/m08-inventory-report-job/starter
cp .env.example .env
npm install
npm run db:deploy                # migrations onto an empty database
npm run db:seed                  # repeatable
npm run dev                      # http://localhost:3108
npm run job:run                  # one pass of the worker, by hand
```

## Where the work is

`src/jobs/report.ts` is the only file you need to change. The inventory
endpoints are carried forward from M06 and M07 and are already correct;
`src/routes/reports.ts` enqueues a job and reads one back, and is also done.
Enqueueing returns **202** and runs nothing inside the request, because a
report over the whole catalogue has no business holding an HTTP connection
open and a caller who disconnects must not cancel work that was accepted.

## The two check commands

```bash
npm run check:baseline   # must pass now: one clean run writes the right report
npm run check:mission    # must fail now: the second run
```

Note where the line falls. The baseline pins a single clean run, the numbers
in the report, and the unique index that makes a duplicate detectable at all.
The mission checks are about the second invocation.

## The failure seam

`runReportJob` takes an optional `beforeItem` hook, called before each product
is written. The checks use it to kill a run part-way through; production code
passes nothing. It is there because injecting a failure is the only way to
test a resume, and a seam you can see in the signature is better than a mock
that reaches inside.

Keep the return shape: the checks read `status`, `linesWritten`, `attempts`
and `detail`, and the difference between "I did the work" and "I did nothing"
has to be visible to the caller.
baselineChecks: npm run db:deploy - migrations apply to an empty database, including ReportJob, ReportLine and the unique index on (jobId, productId)
npm run db:seed - repeatable seed of fictional users and products

npm run check:baseline - the unique index rejects a duplicate report line, enqueueing accepts a job with 202 without running it, and one clean run writes a correct line per product; this must pass before you start
npm run check:baseline - the M06 and M07 inventory endpoints still work, so a change to the job cannot quietly break the data it reads
acceptanceCriteria: A rerun after a partial failure completes the job instead of dying on work it already committed.
A rerun writes only the lines that were missing, not the ones already there.
After a failure and a rerun there is exactly one line per product, with the numbers a clean run would have produced.
Both attempts are counted: a resumed job reports two attempts, not one.
A job that already succeeded is skipped, writes nothing, and does not count an attempt.
A failed attempt moves runAfter forward, and a second failure waits longer than the first.
Once attempts reach maxAttempts the job is no longer picked up, and a refused invocation is not counted as an attempt.
A job that ran out of attempts keeps whatever it did commit, for an operator to inspect.
Two concurrent invocations of the same job result in exactly one doing the work and one reporting that it was skipped, with one line per product and one attempt counted.
A failure is reported as a failure, with a message an operator can act on, and never as success.

checklist.label: check:baseline passes and check:mission fails before I change anything
The claim is a single conditional statement, not a read followed by a write
A rerun finishes the remaining work instead of repeating committed work
Re-running a succeeded job does nothing and says so
Attempts are capped and a retry is delayed, using the columns already in the schema
A failed job records why, and keeps what it committed
I can state what is exactly once here and what is at least once

hints: Make the claim one statement. `updateMany` with the old status in its WHERE clause is a conditional update: PostgreSQL locks the row, re-evaluates the condition and tells you how many rows changed. One concurrent worker sees a count of 1 and the other sees 0, and no separate read could have told them apart.

A resume needs one extra query before the loop: which products has this job already written? `reportLine.findMany({ where: { jobId }, select: { productId: true } })`. Skip those. Note what this is not - it is not what prevents duplicates, the unique index is; it is what lets the job make progress.

Decide what state a failed attempt leaves behind, and use the columns that are already there. `runAfter` is when a SCHEDULER should next consider the job; `attempts` against `maxAttempts` is whether it should be considered at all. Leaving a job on `running` after a failure is the one choice that makes it unrecoverable.
items.solutionMarkdown:
Four changes, and each one moves a decision out of the code's timing and into
the database.

**The claim is one statement.** `updateMany`, with `status in (pending,
failed)` and `attempts < maxAttempts` in the WHERE clause, returns a count.
Exactly one of two concurrent workers sees 1. The read-then-write version
could not be fixed by reordering, because the decision was being made in the
gap between two round trips.

**A rerun resumes.** One query for the `productId`s this job has already
committed, and the loop skips them. That query is the whole difference between
a resume and a repeat - and it is worth being precise about its job: the
unique index on `(jobId, productId)` is what makes a duplicate impossible;
this query is what stops the job dying on its own past work.

**Failure sets a backoff and respects a cap.** `runAfter` moves forward by a
doubling delay so a failing job does not spin, and the attempt cap lives in
the claim, so an exhausted job simply stops being claimable. Nothing needed a
new column.

**A succeeded job is not claimable**, so running it again is a no-op that does
not touch the attempt counter. "I did nothing" and "I did the work" are
different answers and a caller has to be able to tell them apart.

**What is guaranteed, stated carefully.** The committed effect is exactly
once: each `(jobId, productId)` line is written one time, however many
invocations it took. The invocation is at-least-once and always will be. The
solution says so in its own header comment, because a delivery guarantee
written down somewhere nobody reads is not a guarantee.

**One limitation, stated rather than hidden.** A process that dies while
holding a claim leaves the job on `running`, and nothing here picks it up
again. Recovering that needs a lease with an expiry and a heartbeat, which is
a bigger mechanism than this mission. The stuck job was chosen deliberately
over reclaiming on a timeout: a job that needs a human is visible, whereas a
timeout that is too short puts two workers on one job, which is the bug that
was just fixed. M12 builds the same job in C# and asks the same question about
cancellation.
reflectionRubric: I can explain why a conditional update is a different kind of thing from a read followed by a write, and name what the database does that my code cannot.
I can distinguish the query that makes a resume possible from the constraint that makes duplication impossible.
I can defend the state I leave a failed job in, and say what would go wrong in the alternative.
I can state the delivery guarantee in terms of effects rather than invocations, and say what is still at-least-once.
I can describe the failure mode my solution does not handle, and what it would take to handle it.
